newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Commission to recommend limited nickel in euros.
newsitem.headline: Commission to recommend limited nickel in euros.

text.p: The European Commission, responding to concerns about allergies, is to recommend that new euro coins contain only limited amounts of nickel, European Union officials said on Tuesday.
A proposal to be discussed by the EU executive on Thursday would restrict the use of nickel to at most three of the planned eight single currency coins due to be introduced in 2002.
Some coins would instead be made with the metal alloy called "Nordic Gold".

Demand for metal for the new coins could be substantial Although it is not yet known which of the EU's 15 countries will adopt the currency, there is a potential for as many as 70 billion coins to be minted.

EU sources said the Commission proposal, which must eventually be agreed by EU finance ministers, calls for nickel to be withheld from at least two of the planned 10-, 20-, and 50 euro-cents coins, using Nordic Gold instead.
The planned one-, two- and five-cent coins would be made of copper-covered steel, according to the proposal.
Larger denomination one- and two- euro coins would contain some nickel, but EU sources said the Commission had sharply scaled back the content from what is found in current coinage.
Nordic Gold has no gold in it despite the name. It consists mainly of copper and is produced by Finnish metal group Outokumpu.
Sweden has been lobbying against the use of nickel because of health concerns.

Its finance ministry cites figures showing that 20 percent of young women in Europe are affected by nickel allergy, partly because of frequent exposure to the metal, for example by wearing earrings and other jewellery.
Sources said a number of commissioners were expected to push for even less nickel to be used when the issue was discussed on Thursday.
France is a major nickel producer through its New Caledonia territory in the South Pacific where the Eramet mining group is a large player.
Canada, Russia and Australia are major mining areas, while Norway, a non-EU member of the European Economic Area, has a sizeable smelting presence.
Nickel was trading at $7,450 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange on Tuesday.
